newsitem.title: USA: Blue Note loses Internet trademark case.
newsitem.headline: Blue Note loses Internet trademark case.

text.p: A federal judge Monday dismissed a trademark lawsuit brought by New York's legendary Blue Note jazz club against a Missouri college nightspot with the same name that is promoted on the Internet.
An issue raised by the suit is whether a Web site creator is necessarily seeking national customers just because he places promotional information on the Internet.

U.S. District Judge Sidney Stein, who sits in Manhattan federal court, dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction after finding that the owner of the Missouri club was only trying to attract local patrons.

The lawsuit was filed by Bensusan Restaurant Corp., the creator of New York's Blue Note and the owner of its trademark. The defendant in the case is Richard King, who owns the smaller Blue Note nightclub in Columbia, Missouri, that is primarily patronised by University of Missouri students.

King began using the name Blue Note for his club in 1980 and Bensusan registered the trademark in 1985. Because King had used the name first, he had a common law right to keep the name but only in the local Missouri area.

In April, King posted a site on the Internet containing general information about the Missouri club as well as a calendar of events and ticketing information. The site also contained a disclaimer that it was not related to the New York club.

Bensusan argued that by placing the information on the Internet, King had expanded his use of the name outside of Missouri. The corporation argued that King could be held liable in New York because state law permits a court to exercise personal jurisdiction over any non-resident who commits a civil wrong within the state.
Stein said the issue was whether the creation of the Web site with a telephone number to order the allegedly infringing product is an offer to sell the product in New York.
The judge said there was no allegation or proof that any tickets were shipped to New York or that any other wrongful activity occurred here.

King had submitted an affidavit stating that 99 percent of his revenue comes from local residents who are primarily University of Missouri students. Most of his out-of-state customers have either an existing or prior connection to the area.
Even if New Yorkers wanted to buy tickets, they would have to call a Missouri box office and then travel to Missouri to pick up the tickets because King does not mail them out, the judge said.

"The mere fact that a person can gain information on the allegedly infringing product is not the equivalent of a person advertising, promoting, selling or otherwise making an effort to target its product in New York," Stein said.
